questions.q: What is a SOC 2 report, strictly speaking?
options: A government-issued compliance certificate
A self-attestation checklist a vendor fills out with no external review
An independent CPA firm's attestation report on a service organization's controls — not a certification or logo
A one-time penetration test summary
questions.explain: SOC 2 is an AICPA attestation framework. A licensed CPA firm performs the audit and issues a report with an opinion — there is no SOC 2 certificate or badge a company is formally awarded.

questions.q: Which Trust Services Criterion is mandatory in every SOC 2 report, regardless of scope?
options: Privacy
Security
Processing Integrity
Availability
questions.explain: Security (the common criteria covering logical and physical access protection) is required in every SOC 2 engagement. Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, and Privacy are added only when relevant to the service.

questions.q: What does a SOC 2 Type I report actually examine?
options: Whether controls are suitably designed as of a single specified point in time
Whether controls operated effectively over a full 12-month period
Whether the organization has ever had a security incident
Whether the organization's pricing is competitive
questions.explain: Type I tests control design as of one date — whether the controls, if operated as described, would meet their objective. It does not test whether they actually ran that way over time.

questions.q: During Type II fieldwork, what is an auditor primarily doing to test a control like access revocation on termination?
options: Accepting the control owner's verbal confirmation that the policy is followed
Reading the written policy document and treating that as sufficient evidence
Pulling a sample of actual terminated employees and checking system-generated logs for when access was actually revoked
Waiting for the vendor's marketing team to confirm compliance
questions.explain: Type II auditors test operating effectiveness with sampled evidence — actual tickets, logs, and timestamps across the review period — not self-reported claims or policy text alone.

questions.q: A Type II SOC 2 report for a payment processor lists two noted exceptions found during the review period. What does this most reasonably suggest?
options: The report is worthless and the vendor should be immediately disqualified
This is a realistic outcome of real sampling-based testing, not necessarily a disqualifying signal on its own
The auditor made an error and the report should be reissued with zero exceptions
SOC 2 does not allow any exceptions, so the report is invalid
questions.explain: Real Type II reports commonly contain a small number of noted exceptions from sampling; a report with zero exceptions across every sample and every month is unusual enough to warrant extra scrutiny, not automatically trusted more.
